story.text: ## Remote authority is a Chain whose deciding link is elsewhere

A decision about a locale that is made outside it arrives through a chain. Tenant to property manager to management company to the fund that owns the building to the capital behind the fund. Neighborhood need to city department to state agency to federal rule to appropriation. Five links, six, more.
Two things follow from the arithmetic, and they are the whole problem.

The first is ordinary: `BC = B̄ − ln N`. The chain is weak, and it gets weaker with every link. Long remote chains fail often, and they fail silently, because a break anywhere upstream looks from the locale like nothing happening.

The second is the one that matters. **The links that decide are not local, so the people in the locale cannot re-wire the chain.** Everything in [[The Group Of Five]] depends on a group being able to change its own composition when the problem changes. A group that cannot re-wire has exactly one mode available to it — the one it was placed in by somebody else — and that mode is a chain, and it is at the far weak end of it.

This is what "out of the game" means in composition terms. Not that civil society is weak. That it has been composed into an arrangement it does not control, in the mode with the worst arithmetic, at the end furthest from the decision.
## Which makes it domination, mechanically

[[Freedom Participation Solidarity]] gives the test: solidarity without participation is domination. A chain is solidarity — mutual reliance, shared exposure to one another's failure. A chain nobody in the locale chose to be in, and nobody in the locale can leave or alter, is solidarity without participation.

That is not a rhetorical flourish laid over the arithmetic. It is the same statement twice. Wright's Chain is the mode that requires everyone to hold and punishes any deviation. Imposed from outside, that description *is* domination, and no additional political premise is needed to get there.
## Why adding a local coordinator does not fix it
The standard remedy is a liaison, a navigator, a community engagement officer, a coordinating role sitting between the locale and the remote apparatus.

`−ln 5 = −1.61`. `−ln 6 = −1.79`. **The coordinator is another link.** A role introduced to strengthen the connection lengthens the thing it was hired to strengthen, and leaves the deciding link exactly as far away as it was.

The same applies to consultation, to advisory boards, and to any arrangement that adds a station on the path without moving where the decision is made. If the deciding link stays remote, the chain has grown.
## What relocalizing means arithmetically
There are only two moves the arithmetic permits, and "ReLocalize" names both.

**Shorten the chain by bringing the deciding link inside the locale.** Not consultation on a decision made elsewhere — the decision. Every link removed is worth `ln N − ln(N−1)`, and the links worth removing most are the ones between the locale and the decision.

**Convert chain segments into local packs.** Where a single remote route now exists, put several local attempts, first success wins. This is the move that changes the sign: `−ln N` becomes `+ln(N·W)`. And it is the only composition whose strength does not depend on knowing `D`, which matters because nobody remote has ever calibrated the difficulty of a local problem correctly.
## The diversity that makes this work is already there
The obvious objection is that a handful of neighbours cannot match a professional apparatus. Wright's arithmetic says otherwise, and [[What Wright Assumed]] carries the numbers.

Pack strength is `ln(N_eff · W)`, where `N_eff` deflates with `ρ`, the correlation in approach. Five people trained on one protocol, supervised by one person, working from one evidence base sit around `ρ = 0.7` — worth about **+0.27** logits between them, barely more than one person acting alone. Five neighbours who share a locale but not a training, a livelihood, a network or a class position sit near `ρ = 0.1` — worth about **+1.27**, and more once `W` is counted, because heterogeneity raises pack strength directly.
The local group wins by roughly a logit, for precisely the reason the professional team was assembled: uniformity. Shared training makes carbon copies, and a pack of carbon copies is a pack of one.

This is not an argument that expertise is worthless. It is an argument about *where expertise should sit in the composition* — in the standard processes a pack has already discovered and written down (see [[Discovering Standard Processes]]), not in the membership of the pack that has to face what is not yet standard.
## What "back in the game" would look like

A locale where the deciding link is local. A standing group of about five, diverse by circumstance rather than by recruitment policy, that can name which mode it is in and change it. Packs run at problems nobody has solved. Chains kept short and local. Teams convened only on work already made easy, and only by people who were in the pack.
That group is not weaker than the remote apparatus it replaces. On hard problems — the only ones that matter here — it is stronger, and Wright wrote down why in 1995.

story.text: ## A referral pathway is a Chain, and coordination lengthens it

Primary care to specialty to prior authorisation to scheduling to the person actually arriving is five links. `BC = B̄ − ln 5 = B̄ − 1.61` logits. One break loses the person, and every link is a place to break.

The important consequence is counter-intuitive and it is why so many pathway fixes disappoint. **Adding a care coordinator makes it six links: −1.79.** The coordinator is another link. A role introduced to strengthen a pathway lengthens the thing it was hired to strengthen. The only moves the arithmetic permits are removing links, or converting a segment into a Pack — several routes, first success wins.
This is directly encodable in LOP mode: composition as an edge property, with the `ln N` cost computed along each serial run.
## A CHW deployment is a Pack, and eight is the number
The same person, the same need, composed as a Pack of eight community health workers: `+ln 8 = +2.08` logits. A 3.7 logit swing over the chain, from the same people and the same problem.
Eight is not arbitrary. To cover a problem two logits above the group's mean ability you need `ln N > 2`, so `N ≥ 8`. That is the sizing question answered in a form a budget conversation can use.
The Pack also does something the Chain cannot: its strength is independent of problem difficulty. Nobody has to estimate `D` correctly in advance for the arrangement to work.
## Coalitions are Teams pointed at the wrong problems

Community coalitions, task forces and steering committees are Teams. They are convened against precisely the problems where `B̄ − D` is most negative — the region [[The Crossover]] shows to be the one place Teams perform worst of the three.

This is a mathematical case for the NDC and CHW model over the coalition model, and it does not depend on anyone's opinion of coalitions. A Team below `−ln N / (N − 1)` is the worst available option, and its failure mode has a name.
## The standardisation caveat
Pack strength rises with member heterogeneity through the `W` term. Wright also observes that "the homeostasis of most groups induces homogeneity" — groups spontaneously decay into bad Packs.

Healthcare quality machinery pushes uniformly toward homogeneity. That is correct for Chains and for Teams, and destructive for Packs. Knowing which composition you are standardising is the difference between raising `B` and collapsing `W`.
## One care plan holds all three
Inside a single Shared Care Plan all three compositions are present, and confusing them is the standard failure.

Medication reconciliation is a **Chain** — one break harms, danger looms, and Wright's guidance is explicit that when danger looms, commitment to maintained agreement is safer. Finding what actually helps this particular person is a **Pack** — a hard problem, upside-dominated, where people should be trying different things. Agreeing the goals the person themselves holds is a **Team**, and it is legitimate only to the degree the person genuinely participated in it — see [[Freedom Participation Solidarity]].

Running discovery through chain-governance kills it. Running safety through pack-autonomy hurts people. Treating a plan the person did not participate in as consensus produces a mob of two. That distinction is nameable, and it is enforceable in the SCP plugins.
The same argument at the scale of governance and property, rather than of care, is [[Civil Society Back In The Game]].

story.text: At the foot of Wright's 1996 page there is a sentence: "Only when problems can be made easy, because we have become better able to manage them, can Team-work succeed." Marc's margin, in red, glosses it: **discovering standard processes**.

That gloss is the most valuable thing on the page, and it is not Wright's. Wright treats "problems become easy" as something that simply happens. Naming the mechanism turns a description into a control loop.

story.text: ## The loop
A **Pack** goes out at a problem harder than the people facing it. Many attempts, deliberately different, first success wins, failures cost nothing.
**What worked** is one member's success. It is still an anecdote. It has lowered `D` for nobody.

A **standard process** is that success named, written and taught. This is the only lever anyone actually has, because you cannot raise `B` quickly and you cannot choose an easier world. Standardising is how `D` comes down.

With `D` down, the work is specifiable, so it can be handed off — a **Chain**, kept as short as the arithmetic demands. And with `D` below the group's average `B`, consensus finally becomes the strongest composition: a **Team**, which is a *reward* for having made the problem easy, not a way of attacking it.

The **control chart** is what tells you whether the problem is still easy. A process in control is the empirical signature of a `D` that has stayed down. A **special cause** says `D` has risen or `B` has fallen, the group is no longer entitled to Team-work, and the loop reopens.
## Why this is an SPC argument
Pack → Chain → Team is not a maturity model that a group climbs once. It is a control loop, and statistical process control is its instrumentation.

This connects Wright to a practice already in the toolset rather than adding a new one. The rational subgroup and Wright's composition analysis are the same argument in two dialects: **aggregation is not neutral, and the wrong aggregation destroys the signal.** A control chart drawn over a Pack and a control chart drawn over a Chain are charting different variables even when the raw counts are identical.

The uncomfortable corollary, in Wright's own words, is that a Team working a problem that has not been made easy is a mob. Most healthcare committees are exactly that: consensus bodies convened against problems far above their `B̄`, in the one region where the arithmetic says consensus performs worst of all three.
## SODOTO is the other blade

Standardising lowers `D`. Teaching raises `B`. Both close the same gap, and See One / Do One / Teach One is how a standard process actually propagates — an unwritten, untaught practice lowers `D` for nobody.

That reframes SODOTO usefully. It does not organise the group. It moves `B`, and moving `B` is what changes which composition is optimal. It is the mechanism by which a Pack earns the right to become a Team.
## RenDanHeYi, exactly here

Wright's closing practical note is that productive consensus-building "requires that each difficult task be divided into several easy tasks, so that there is a high probability that each group member, acting alone, would have made the consensus-decision."

That is 单 — the concrete single order — sized so that Team-work is genuinely the optimal composition rather than an aspiration. Haier's zero-distance is the Chain-shortening move standing next to it. Both are the same operation Wright describes: get `D` under `B̄` before asking anyone to agree.

That reframes SODOTO usefully. It does not organise the group. It moves `B`, and moving `B` is what changes which composition is optimal. It is the mechanism by which a Pack earns the right to become a Team.
## RenDanHeYi, exactly here

Wright's closing practical note is that productive consensus-building "requires that each difficult task be divided into several easy tasks, so that there is a high probability that each group member, acting alone, would have made the consensus-decision."

That is 单 — the concrete single order — sized so that Team-work is genuinely the optimal composition rather than an aspiration. Haier's zero-distance is the Chain-shortening move standing next to it. Both are the same operation Wright describes: get `D` under `B̄` before asking anyone to agree.

story.text: On the last page of the annotated paper there is a small red drawing: three circles marked **F**, **P** and **S**, with **Team** written above, **Pack** at the lower left and **Chain** at the lower right. Freedom, Participation, Solidarity.

Marc has told this story elsewhere. Asked in a facilitated circle to say what he cared most about, he heard himself say "freedom and solidarity" and had no idea what he meant. Years of puzzling produced the answer that the load-bearing word was the conjunction, and that **AND = PARTICIPATION** — see [[Freedom AND Solidarity]] and [[Freedom AND Solidarity as ReLocalize Creativity]].

That frame gives three tests. Solidarity without participation is domination. Freedom without participation is isolation. Freedom and solidarity together require participation in all decision-making that affects others.
## Wright supplies the mechanics
The correspondence is close, and one leg of it is Wright's own word rather than an interpretation laid over him.
A **Pack** is Freedom. Members try different things, no agreement is required of anyone, and a member who fails costs the Pack nothing. Maximum individual latitude, structurally guaranteed.

A **Chain** is Solidarity. Wright's sentence is "A Chain relies on solidarity. It works when everyone is in lock step, but it fails when any member stumbles." Mutual reliance, and mutual exposure to one another's failure.
A **Team** is what participation makes possible — the state in which freedom and solidarity are held at once, which is why it sits at the top of the drawing rather than beside the other two.
## The three pathologies
What makes this more than a tidy analogy is that Wright independently produces the failure modes, including one the frame does not name.

**Freedom without participation is isolation.** In Wright's terms, a Pack that never converges. When the Chain disintegrates, he writes, "the former members are forced to fend for themselves." Endless divergence, nothing ever built.

**Solidarity without participation is domination.** A Chain that nobody chose to be in. Lock step imposed rather than undertaken — and Wright's defensive branch, "circle the wagons, regress to a previous Chain in desperate hope of weathering the storm," which he says destroys the Team when it fails.

**Consensus without participation is a mob.** This is the one the frame does not name and Wright does: "A mob is a Team that chooses the wrong solution to a difficult social problem." A Team that skipped the Pack phase is domination wearing consensus clothing, and the arithmetic says it will be the worst of the three available options.
## What that makes of the sequence

Pack → Chain → Team stops being a maturity model that groups climb once and becomes **the path participation has to walk for freedom and solidarity to be co-possible**. Each shortcut has a name and a named pathology. You cannot start at Team; a Team assembled without the Pack phase is a mob by construction.

This is also why the Quaker Friends Meeting is the right reference. What happens there, in Marc's description, is "not agreement or consensus — it is global understanding," Follett's whole in every part. In Wright's terms that is the requirement to run the Pack long enough, and honestly enough, before anyone is entitled to the Team.
## Cave drawings are the participation mechanism

The ReLocalize Creativity page names cave drawings as the instrument of synthesis: explicit, evolving models that make everyone's mental models visible, comparable and discussable, built not to analyse a system but to get the whole into every part.

Read against Wright, that is a precise functional claim. **The cave drawing is what lets a Pack's scattered findings become a Chain and then a Team without anyone being coerced into agreement.** It is how the transition happens participatively rather than by authority — which is to say, it is the thing that keeps solidarity from becoming domination on the way up.

The Ethical Regulator Theorem sits in the same place. Ashby's requirement that every good regulator be a model of the system could just as easily license technocratic control — solidarity without participation. It becomes participatory self-regulation only when the modelling itself is participatory. See [[Requisite Variety]] for the variety-matching half of that argument, of which Wright's `(B̄ − D)` is the scalar form.
What this looks like in practice, and how small a group it takes, is [[The Group Of Five]].
The case where solidarity-without-participation is not a risk but the standing arrangement is [[Civil Society Back In The Game]].

story.text: In the 1920s the physicist Norman Campbell argued that you cannot measure a social variable, because you cannot concatenate people. Length is measurable because sticks lie end to end. Weight is measurable because bricks pile up. People, Campbell said, do no such thing, and so social science has no metre stick.

Benjamin Wright's answer, seventy years later, was that people are concatenated constantly — we just do it under three different rules, and each rule has its own arithmetic. Once you write the arithmetic down, group organisation stops being a matter of temperament and becomes something you can calculate.

story.text: ## The three rules

A **Team** wins when everyone agrees and the agreement is right. A two-member team has only two outcomes available to it, (11) and (00) — the rules of Team behaviour eliminate disagreement entirely. Juries work this way. So do committees, steering groups, and every consensus body ever convened.

A **Pack** wins when any single member succeeds. Members are supposed to try different things; helpful disagreements (10) and (01) are what the Pack runs on, and (11) is eliminated because two people doing the same thing is not Pack behaviour. Search parties work this way. So does the immune system, and so does Darwinian evolution.

A **Chain** loses when any single member fails. Perfect agreement (11) wins, either disagreement loses, and (00) cannot occur. Referral pathways work this way. So do supply chains, hand-offs, and every process where one dropped ball loses the whole thing.
## The arithmetic that follows
Applying Rasch model odds to each rule gives three laws. Write Bn for a person's ability, D for the difficulty of the problem, and N for the number of people.

**Team:** `BT − D = Σ (Bn − D)`. Strength *relative to the task*, accumulated linearly. Task difficulty enters the sum N times. A member more able than the problem adds; a member less able than the problem subtracts, by their full deficit. Wright's dry note: more is often not better, as has been frequently observed about committees.

**Pack:** `BP = B̄ + ln(N·W)`. Absolute strength, accumulated exponentially. Task difficulty does not appear at all. Adding a member always helps. The `W` term rises with the spread of member abilities, so heterogeneity helps too.
**Chain:** `BC = B̄ − ln N`. Weakness accumulated exponentially. Task difficulty does not appear here either. Adding a link always hurts. There is no length at which a chain stops bleeding.
## What the laws do to the same ten people
Wright's own example. Ten people, each 1 logit *below* the difficulty of the task in front of them.
As a Team they are `10 × (−1) = −10.0` logits. As a Chain, `−1 − ln 10 = −3.3`. As a Pack, `−1 + ln 10 = +1.3`.

The same ten people, facing the same problem, are catastrophic, mediocre, or sufficient — depending on nothing but how they are wired together. That is the whole claim, and it is worth sitting with before going further, because almost every convening decision in community health is made without anyone asking which of the three is being built.
## Where this goes
[[The Crossover]] gives the threshold — the exact point at which one composition overtakes another, and the group-size rule that falls out of it.

[[Discovering Standard Processes]] is the part Wright left implicit and Marc named in the margin: problems do not become easy by themselves, and the thing that makes them easy is the only real lever anyone has.
[[Composing A Neighborhood]] applies the three laws to referral pathways, CHW deployment, and the Shared Care Plan.

[[The Group Of Five]] is Marc's own speculation, and the most actionable page here: a standing group of about five, re-wired rather than re-staffed, learns all three modes and arrives at Follett's synthesis as a by-product.

[[Civil Society Back In The Game]] is why any of this matters: remote government and remote landlords are a Chain whose deciding link sits outside the locale, and relocalizing is the only move the arithmetic allows.
[[Freedom Participation Solidarity]] decodes the three-circle drawing in the margin of the last page, and is where Wright's arithmetic meets Marc's own frame.
[[What Wright Assumed]] is the honest accounting of where the model's assumptions do not survive contact with real groups, and what to do about it.

Sources: Benjamin D. Wright, "Teams, Packs and Chains", *Rasch Measurement Transactions* 1995, 9:2 p.432; "Pack to Chain to Team", *RMT* 1996, 10:2 p.501; and MESA Memo 67, "Composition Analysis", which carries the derivations.

story.text: Wright's three laws each say "more" or "less", but the useful question is *when*. At what point does one composition overtake another? The algebra answers exactly, and the answer is a single expression that turns out to be the most portable thing in the paper.
## The threshold
Setting Team strength equal to Pack strength and solving gives the condition under which a Team is worth building at all.
A Team beats a Pack when `B̄ − D > ln N / (N − 1)`. Below `−ln N / (N − 1)`, the Team is not merely second best — it is the *worst* of the three, behind even the Chain.

Between those two curves is Pack country, and it is wider than anyone's instinct suggests. Note what the threshold is not: it is not zero. Being merely as able as the problem is not enough to justify consensus. A group must be measurably *better* than its problem before agreement outperforms diversity.
## The size rule

Marc's marginal note on the figure reads: **chain ↑ · Team ← Magic # 3 · ↓ packs maybe (too small)**. That is a size rule read off a chart drawn about difficulty, and the arithmetic supports all three arrows.

**Chains: as short as possible.** Every link costs `ln N`. Three links is −1.10 logits, five is −1.61, ten is −2.30. The penalty is unbounded and there is no length at which it stops. The only design move available is fewer links.

**Teams: around three.** A team of three must average 0.55 logits above the problem to beat a pack of three. That threshold actually *falls* as N grows — a group of ten needs only 0.26 — but the binding constraint is the other law: `Σ(Bn − D)` subtracts the full deficit of every member below the problem. Big teams survive only on easy problems. Three is about where teams stay honest.

**Packs: bigger than three.** Marc's scepticism is right and there is a number for it. Pack gain is `ln N`, so covering a problem two logits above the group's mean ability requires `ln N > 2`, meaning **N ≥ 8**. Three logits needs N ≥ 20. A pack of three buys 1.10 logits and no more.
The counterweight is diminishing returns. Going from two to three members buys 0.41 logits; going from nine to ten buys 0.11. Packs are cheap to build up to about eight and expensive past it.
## The one to keep in front of you
Pack strength contains no `D` term at all. Team strength contains `D` N times over.

This is the practical difference. **A Pack is the only composition whose strength you can state without knowing how hard the problem is.** In neighborhood work, where nobody can honestly calibrate difficulty in advance, that is not a technicality — it is the argument for defaulting to Pack organisation whenever you are genuinely uncertain, and reserving Team organisation for problems you have already made easy.
See [[Discovering Standard Processes]] for what "already made easy" costs.

story.text: Wright treats composition as a property a group *has*. The more useful reading, and the one Marc was reaching for in the margin, is that composition is a repertoire a group *learns* — and that a standing group of about five, cycling through all three modes as the problem in front of it changes, will develop two things without being taught either.

The first is fluency in all three modes. The second, and the one that matters more, is Follett's participation: the whole in every part and every part in the whole, arrived at as synthesis rather than compromise.

story.text: ## Why five

Wright supplies no number, so this is speculation checked against his arithmetic rather than derived from it. What the arithmetic does say is that five is roughly where all three modes are simultaneously *practicable*.

A pack of five is worth `+ln 5 = +1.61` logits — enough to take on a problem a good distance above the group's mean ability, which is the whole point of packing. A pack of three is worth only `+1.10`, which is thin; you would rarely reach for it.
A team of five needs to average only `+0.40` logits over its problem to be the right choice. That is a reachable bar on work the group has already standardised.

A chain of five costs `−1.61` logits, which is bad but survivable, and five links is a realistic length — it is the length of an actual referral pathway. At ten the penalty is `−2.30` and chain practice becomes mostly a lesson in failure. At ten, too, a team must keep every one of ten members above `D`, which almost never holds.
So below five the pack is too weak to be worth running, and above five the chain and the team stop being genuinely available. Five is where a group can really do all three.

There is a second reason. The gap between the best and worst mode is `2 ln N` — at five, 3.22 logits. That is large enough that choosing the wrong composition visibly hurts, and therefore large enough to learn from, while the group is still small enough that every member occupies every position in every mode.
## What each mode teaches
This is the part that does the real work, and it is why cycling produces Follett rather than merely producing competence.

**A Pack teaches that the parts make up the whole.** Its rule requires each member to try something no one else is trying. Every person spends the pack phase being a genuinely distinct part, holding a piece nobody else holds, and watching the group's outcome assembled out of those separate pieces. Failure costs nothing, so the distinctness is safe.

**A Chain teaches that the whole is in every part.** Its rule is that one break loses everything. Every person spends the chain phase carrying the entire outcome, because the entire outcome does in fact live in each link. Nobody can be a fraction of the result; each is the whole of it.

**A Team is where the two arrive together.** Nothing happens until all agree, so the decision is at once one thing the group holds and something every member holds entirely. That is not compromise, which splits the difference between parts, and not consensus in the thin sense of everyone assenting. ## What follows for practice
A neighborhood team should be composed once, at about five, and then *re-wired* repeatedly rather than re-staffed. The unit of design is the mode, not the membership.

Rotation matters. If the same person is always the first link, or always the one whose idea the pack adopts, the group learns the modes but not the participation — some members will have experienced only being a part and others only carrying the whole. Everyone occupies every position, which at five is arithmetically possible and at twelve is not.

The switch itself should be explicit and named. "We are packing this" and "this is a chain, so keep it short" are the two most useful sentences available to a standing group, and they are only sayable once the modes have names.

And the sequence is not optional. [[Freedom Participation Solidarity]] sets out why: Pack → Chain → Team is the path participation has to walk, and each shortcut has a pathology. The group of five is the smallest vehicle that can actually walk it.

This is where [[Discovering Standard Processes]] and this page meet. A group of five cycling the modes is simultaneously running the discovery loop — packing at hard problems, standardising what worked, chaining the handoffs, teaming on what has been made easy — and building the mutual understanding that lets it do so without anyone being coerced. The loop produces capability; the cycling produces the participation that makes the capability legitimate.

The more useful reading, and the one Marc was reaching for in the margin, is that composition is a repertoire a group *learns* — and that a standing group of about five, cycling through all three modes as the problem in front of it changes, will develop two things without being taught either.

DIAGRAM_wright-five-and-follett
## Why five

Wright supplies no number, so this is speculation checked against his arithmetic rather than derived from it. What the arithmetic does say is that five is roughly where all three modes are simultaneously *practicable*.

A pack of five is worth `+ln 5 = +1.61` logits — enough to take on a problem a good distance above the group's mean ability, which is the whole point of packing. A pack of three is worth only `+1.10`, which is thin; you would rarely reach for it.
A team of five needs to average only `+0.40` logits over its problem to be the right choice. That is a reachable bar on work the group has already standardised.

A chain of five costs `−1.61` logits, which is bad but survivable, and five links is a realistic length — it is the length of an actual referral pathway. At ten the penalty is `−2.30` and chain practice becomes mostly a lesson in failure. At ten, too, a team must keep every one of ten members above `D`, which almost never holds.
So below five the pack is too weak to be worth running, and above five the chain and the team stop being genuinely available. Five is where a group can really do all three.

There is a second reason. The gap between the best and worst mode is `2 ln N` — at five, 3.22 logits. story.text: Composition analysis is worth taking into RCN work, which means it is worth being honest about where its assumptions do not survive contact with real groups.
## Conditional independence is the load-bearing assumption

Every derivation assumes members succeed or fail independently, given ability `B` and difficulty `D`. Real groups have correlated errors, and correlated error is not a minor perturbation — it is the one correction that changes the numbers materially.

The usual way to write it is a design-effect deflation: `N_eff = N / (1 + ρ(N − 1))`, where `ρ` is the correlation in *approach* — how likely two members are to try the same thing. Pack gain is then `ln(N_eff · W)` rather than `ln(N · W)`.
What matters is which groups this actually penalises. For a group of five:
**ρ:** 0.1 — **effective N:** 3.57 — **pack gain:** +1.27 — **who this describes:** diverse neighbours in a shared locale
**ρ:** 0.3 — **effective N:** 2.27 — **pack gain:** +0.82 — **who this describes:** same locale, some shared habits
**ρ:** 0.5 — **effective N:** 1.67 — **pack gain:** +0.51 — **who this describes:** same employer, same orientation
**ρ:** 0.7 — **effective N:** 1.32 — **pack gain:** +0.27 — **who this describes:** an identically trained cohort

**The correction bites hardest on professionals.** Five people trained on one protocol, supervised by one person, working from one evidence base are close to `ρ = 0.7` — worth about a quarter of a logit between them, barely more than one person acting alone. Five neighbours who share a locale but not a training, a class position, a network or a livelihood sit near the top of that table.

So the honest reading is the opposite of the one usually offered. Diversity is not a nicety to be engineered into a pack after the fact; it is the thing that makes a pack a pack, and the professionalised team is the degenerate case. Wright's `W` term points the same way — pack strength rises with member heterogeneity, and a cohort selected for uniformity has `W ≈ 1` while a genuinely mixed neighborhood group has `W > 1`.

This is why [[Civil Society Back In The Game]] is a composition argument rather than a political preference. A local group of five out-packs a trained team of five on Wright's own arithmetic, by about a logit, for exactly the reason the trained team was assembled.

The correction runs the other way for Chains, with the same sign of surprise. Correlated links fail together — one funding cut, one outage, one policy change takes out several at once — so `−ln N` *understates* chain fragility rather than overstating it.
## The model is silent about time

There is no cost of delay anywhere in the arithmetic. A Pack of eight all trying different things takes longer than a Chain of five executing a known process, and in clinical work the delay is itself harm.
Wright is comparing probabilities of success on a single task, not throughput or latency. Any operational use has to add that separately.
## Ability is one number

`Bn` is a scalar on one variable. The whole apparatus rests on a Rasch model in which the persons and the tasks are on a single dimension. Community health problems are conspicuously not unidimensional, and a person strong on one facet may be weak on another. In a diverse local group that is a feature — it is most of where the low `ρ` comes from — but it does mean a single `B̄` is a coarse summary.

Many-facet Rasch measurement is Wright's own answer to this, and MESA Memo 67 works the compositions through it — Packs and Chains turn out not to care about the levels of other facets, which is convenient. But the single-number version used on the other pages here is a simplification, and worth flagging as one.
## Nobody has calibrated D

Every practical statement of the form "this group is 0.6 logits below this problem" presumes a calibration nobody has performed. In the absence of one, the results still carry ordinal weight — chains get worse with length, packs get better, teams need to out-match their problem — but the specific numbers are illustrative.
This is an argument for the Pack default rather than against the framework. Pack strength is the only one of the three that does not require knowing `D`.
## What survives all of that

The ordinal claims are robust to every objection above. Adding a link always weakens a chain. Adding a member always strengthens a pack, though correlation may make the gain much smaller than `ln N` suggests. A member below the problem always weakens a team. Consensus on a hard problem is always the worst of the three.

Those hold under any plausible correction, and they are enough to change how a neighborhood organises itself. The precise logits are for later, and probably for the SPC work rather than for this paper.
